title: Extreme Weather Takes a Toll on the Workforce - Deccan Chronicle
full_text:
As floods, heatwaves and cloudbursts become more frequent, millions of workers are losing income, productivity and security
This monsoon, India has witnessed a series of extreme weather events unfolding across different regions almost simultaneously. While flash floods swept through parts of the Northeast, cloudbursts and intense rainfall disrupted life in western India. At the same time, severe heatwave conditions pushed temperatures above 45°C across parts of Rajasthan, Punjab, Haryana and Delhi.
In Assam, floods affected nearly 48,500 people across four districts in early July, according to the Assam State Disaster Manage-ment Authority (ASDMA). Mumbai, meanwhile, grappled with heavy spells of rain that caused widespread waterlogging, disrupted transport services and triggered building collapses.
Worrisome Weather
Nearly 1.16 lakh people were internally displaced in Andhra Pradesh during 2025 due to cyclones and severe storm events. According to the State of India’s Environment 2026 report released by Down To Earth, Andhra Pradesh was one of the worst affected states in the country. Extreme weather events wreaked havoc in AP on 58 days between October and December 2025. It was the second-highest in the country after Himachal Pradesh, which recorded 62 days. These are no longer freak, isolated events. The trend of extreme weather continues in 2026 too.
Meteorologists and climate scientists now describe this convergence with floods, cloudbursts and heatwaves striking simultaneously in different corners of the country, as evidence that extreme weather has become India's new normal instead of an exception. Behind the satellite maps and rainfall statistics lies a quieter and slower-moving crisis, namely the erosion of the country’s workforce to work.
Workforce Under Siege
For India’s roughly 500 million strong workforce, extreme weather is not an abstract policy debate. It is a daily occupational hazard. Nearly half of Indian workers are employed in agriculture, while a significant share of the rest work outdoors in construction, delivery services, street vending, fishing and transport. When floods submerge fields or heat makes it dangerous to step outside, wages stop. “We tend to talk about climate change in terms of glaciers and carbon emissions,” says Dr Sunita Krishnan, an environmental scientist. “But the immediate, measurable damage is to human bodies and human incomes. A mason who cannot lay bricks after 11 a.m. because of heat stress loses pay. A farmer whose field floods twice in one season loses the entire year's income. That is climate change translated into a wage slip.”
Living The Whiplash
In Hyderabad, construction supervisor manager Dilip Kumar says rising temperatures have changed the way his team works. “Because of the intense heat, many labourers cannot continue working through the afternoon. They need frequent breaks, which slows down work and reduces their earning hours,” he says.
In Assam’s Dima Hasao district, farmer Priya Baruah has seen floods destroy her paddy fields repeatedly. Her family has lost three harvests in the past five years as floods have become more frequent and severe. “They can call it climate change or cloudburst or whatever,” she says quietly. “For us, it simply means we don’t know if we’ll have enough to eat next month.”
In Kolkata, shopkeeper Sourav Dey has made his own peace with unpredictability. After last year's cloudburst flooded his neighbourhood for days, he now keeps his goods stored a foot above the ground throughout the year. “We do not wait for warnings anymore. We just prepare, always.”
Reactive, Not Resilient
Is India prepared for what is unfolding? The government has taken visible steps, including early warning systems for cloudbursts, heat action plans in vulnerable cities and expanded weather forecasting. However, experts argue that the response remains reactive instead of structural.
“We are very good at disaster response in India through evacuations, relief camps and rescue operations,” says Dr Krishnan. “What we lack is disaster prevention built into the way we plan cities, design labour laws and protect informal workers. Heat action plans exist on paper in many states, but enforcement, including paid breaks, shaded work zones and compensation for lost wages, remains patchy.”
Socio-Economic Impact
“Every monsoon, we rebuild the same roads, resettle the same villages and act surprised. Resilience is not just about warning people that a flood is coming. It is also about insurance schemes, portable social security for migrant workers and infrastructure that does not wash away every few years,” says Nachiket Yadav, an Economist.
Pointing out to the pothole-ridden roads in Mumbai, India’s financial capital, Sheetal Kulkarni, a school teacher and green activist rues, “Every year it is the same story during the rains, but we learn nothing from it. Our politicians thing concretisation of roads solves the problem. That has led to so many tree-fall incidents this year in Mumbai.” Mumbai has witnessed more than 1,000 tree-fall incidents this year.
However, BMC Commissioner Ashwini Bhide has rubbished the claims of concrete roads being responsible for trees falls saying, “It was due to the strong winds and other factors.” Arborists like Vaibhav Raje and others have repeatedly stressed that extreme weather events contribute significantly to tree falls. “The concrete around trees accelerates root decay,” says Makarand Deshpande, a green activist from Mumbai, but our netas and babus think otherwise.
The Bottom Line
For millions of Indians, climate change is no longer a distant warning. It is reflected in shorter working hours, lost wages and uncertain livelihoods. As extreme weather becomes more frequent, the country’s biggest challenge may not be rebuilding after every disaster, but protecting the people whose work keeps India moving.
Caught In The Vortex
• The year 2024 was the hottest year on record globally, followed by 2023 and 2025.
• Worker productivity drops by 2–3% for every degree above 20°C.
• Health risks include heatstroke, dehydration, kidney dysfunction, and neurological disorders, all of which hinder long-term health and economic security.
• Approximately half the global population suffers adverse consequences of high temperatures.
(Source: World Meteorological Organization)
